claim: Robert Abbott's Chicago Defender ran the 1917 'Great Northern Drive' campaign urging Southern Blacks to migrate to Chicago, and built a Pullman-porter distribution network carrying the paper across the Mason-Dixon Line.
contradictory_evidence: Michaeli's 60,000 WWI figure is single-sourced (PROVISIONAL). Grossman argues labor-market signals, not the press, were the primary migration driver (see CL-004).
evidence: Richardson documents the full-page 1917 'Great Northern Drive' spread and porter distribution; Grossman records circulation 33,000 (1916) to 130,000 (1919); Michaeli reports ~60,000 migrants came to Chicago during WWI alone
notes: Sibling had the Defender's migration role as Provisional; now Supported. Porter-residency claims remain unverified.
source: Allissa V. Richardson, 'The Platform: How Pullman porters used railways to engage in networked journalism' (peer-reviewed); James R. Grossman, 'Land of Hope' (1989); Ethan Michaeli, 'The Defender' (2016)

claim: Migrants responded primarily to wartime industrial labor-market signals (jobs in meatpacking, steel, manufacturing); the Defender amplified and channeled a movement it did not originate.

claim: By the 1930s the Black Belt existed as a narrow ~40-block corridor along both sides of State Street, 'almost completely segregated,' characterized by extreme overcrowding, dilapidated tenements, high rents, and kitchenette apartments; residents' choices were limited by covenants, redlining, and violent protests in nearby white neighborhoods.
evidence: Report text quoted verbatim in search-result capture; describes corridor, overcrowding, kitchenettes, covenants/redlining/violence, and Bronzeville as 'one of the largest black communities in the United States' and 'the center of African-American culture in Chicago'
notes: New source; core evidence for the confinement→concentration thesis (F2). Full PDF should be read directly at next pass (currently via captured text).
source: Chicago Commission on Chicago Landmarks, 'Chicago Black Renaissance Literary Movement' report (chicago.gov)

claim: Bronzeville's post-rise transformation was multi-causal: deindustrialization, deliberate segregation policy, demographic pressure, disinvestment, urban renewal and public-housing siting/demolition, expressway routing, and constrained-then-expanded mobility/outmigration operated together across decades. No single cause (e.g., 'the Dan Ryan killed Bronzeville') is supported.
